prompt: Is it better to have a few close friends or many casual ones? Write an essay with a clear position.
text:
# A Few Close Friends Beat Many Casual Ones

Most people want both kinds of friendship, but if you had to favor one, you should favor depth. A few close friends do more for your health, your character, and your sense of being known than a large circle of acquaintances can.

Start with what close friends give you that casual ones cannot. A close friend is the person you call when your marriage is struggling, when you lose a job, or when you get a frightening diagnosis. You can only make that call if you trust the person to keep what you say private and to care about you more than about how you look. Casual friends are pleasant, but the relationship rests on staying light. Telling them something heavy often feels like breaking an unspoken rule.

The research on well-being points the same way. Long-running studies of adult life, such as the Harvard Study of Adult Development, have found that the quality of a person's close relationships predicts health and happiness in later life better than the number of their contacts. Loneliness is not the same as being alone. People can feel isolated in a crowd of acquaintances, and people with two or three devoted friends often feel well supported.

Time is the other reason. Friendship takes hours, and you only have so many. Anthropologist Robin Dunbar has estimated that people can keep about five very close relationships and about fifteen good ones, with each further layer getting less attention. If you spread yourself across hundreds of people, you will probably know none of them well. Depth is how you spend a limited budget on the relationships that return the most.

Close friendships also change you. A good friend will tell you when you are wrong, remember who you were five years ago, and notice when you are not yourself. Casual friends rarely have the history or the license to do this. They tend to see the version of you that you choose to show, so they cannot help you grow past it.

The case for many casual friends is real, and I do not want to wave it away. Sociologist Mark Granovetter showed that weak ties often bring job leads, new ideas, and introductions that your close circle already knows about. A wide network makes life more interesting and more resilient. But these benefits are mostly practical and occasional. They help you find opportunities. They do not hold you up when things go wrong.

The two kinds are also not equal in cost of loss. If you lose a casual friend, you barely notice. If you lose a close one, it hurts, and that is exactly the point: the hurt measures what the friendship was worth.

So the best approach is to invest first in a small core of people you trust deeply, and let casual friendships fill in around them as time allows. If the choice is forced, choose the few. When life is hard, you will not need a crowd. You will need someone who knows you and picks up the phone.
